mkdir -p docs && cat > docs/brief.md <<'EOF'
# RL Lab

**Status:** Draft · **Last updated:** 2026-10-17

## The problem
I want to learn reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trial and error from rewards. Tutorials show working code but hide why it works and how it breaks. I learn best by building. A few small worlds, each teaching one idea and each built from scratch, would give me understanding I can explain, not just code I copied.

## Who it's for
Me: someone with some neural-network experience who is new to reinforcement learning, working evenings and weekends.

## Goals
1. In every world, a learning agent clearly beats both random play and a simple hand-written rule.
2. I can watch any trained agent play in a replay, and compare it with earlier points in training.
3. For every world, I can explain in my own words why its learning method works and where it struggles.
4. Each new world reuses one shared core (world interface, training loop, logging, replay viewer) instead of starting over.

## Constraints
- I write the core learning algorithms myself. Existing libraries are only for checking my results later.
- A laptop (Apple Silicon, CPU only), with about an hour of training per world. A few dollars of rented GPU time is acceptable if a world truly needs it.
- A few weeks of spare time per world.
- Only simple 2D worlds that the agent sees as numbers, not pictures.

## What success looks like
- Each world has a learning-curve chart showing the agent above both baselines, across several training runs.
- A replay of each trained agent that visibly does the intended thing: the snake eats and avoids itself, the fish dodge the ball, the prey forage while fleeing.
- A short write-up per world, in my own words.

## What we're betting on
- Hand-written algorithms can be made correct enough. Bugs in this kind of learning are silent, so the baselines are the main safety net.
- Small worlds with simple number inputs can be learned within an hour on a laptop.
- One shared core can serve a grid game, smooth movement and two competing teams without bending out of shape.

## Not doing
- 3D physics — the 2D worlds teach the same ideas.
- Learning from screen pixels or Atari games — too slow for a laptop and adds a separate vision problem.
- Reproducing research papers — the goal is understanding, not matching published numbers.
- Web deployment or a hosted demo — replays run locally.
- Chasing top scores — beating the baselines clearly is enough.

## Known risk
- In the predator-prey world, both sides learn at once, so each keeps changing the other's problem. Training may go in circles and never look "solved." Watching and explaining that behavior counts as success there.
EOF
wc -w docs/brief.md

steps.text:
I wrote the draft brief to `docs/brief.md` (444 words, **Status: Draft**). The direction is your plan, three worlds each teaching one concept, built on one shared core.

- **Problem:** tutorials hide why reinforcement learning works and how it breaks, so you want to learn by building small worlds from scratch.
- **Top goal:** in every world, a learning agent clearly beats both random play and a simple hand-written rule, across several training runs.
- **Biggest Not Doing item:** learning from screen pixels or Atari games, which is too slow on a laptop and adds a separate vision problem.

The brief also states that the predator-prey world may never look "solved," and that watching and explaining what happens there still counts as success.

**Roadmap stages I'd add when you accept** (defaults shown):

| Stage | Outline | Skills |
|---|---|---|
| **S1: Snake + shared core** | Train a snake that beats random and rule-based play, watch its replay, using the reusable core (world interface, training loop, logging, replay viewer) | null-hypothesis-testing, dataviz |
| **S2: Fish tank** | Fish learn smooth movement to dodge the bouncing ball, built up from one fish that sees everything, to many fish, to fish that only see nearby things | null-hypothesis-testing, dataviz |
| **S3: Predator-prey** | Prey and predator learn at the same time; you can watch and explain the back-and-forth between them | null-hypothesis-testing, dataviz |

- **null-hypothesis-testing** checks that "beats the baselines" is real across several runs and not luck.
- **dataviz** covers the learning-curve charts.
- No reference files are waiting to be assigned.

I don't size stages. The fish tank's three steps become milestones later, in build-planning.

Want me to add S1–S3 with those skills? **[yes / edit]** Then **accept** the brief, or tell me what to change.
